meta.title: Exercise for Parkinson's Disease
meta.summary: A comprehensive home programme — big movements, fast movements, hard aerobic work and balance training — built on the principles behind PD Warrior and LSVT BIG.

paras: Exercise is not an optional extra in Parkinson's disease. It is the only intervention with any credible evidence of altering the course of the condition rather than merely masking the symptoms, and it improves almost every aspect of it — walking, balance, mood, sleep, constipation, and probably thinking.

But the *type* of exercise matters more here than in almost any other condition. Gentle, comfortable, repetitive exercise is worth very little. What the brain responds to is movement that is **big**, **fast**, **hard**, **complicated** and **meaningful to you** — which is exactly what the PD Warrior and LSVT BIG approaches are built on.

box.title: The central problem this programme is designed to solve
box.text: Parkinson's does not only slow your movements — it recalibrates your sense of how big a movement needs to be. A step that feels normal from the inside is visibly small from the outside. That is why you cannot simply be told to 'take bigger steps': you have to be trained to produce movements that feel excessive, because those are the ones that look and function normally.

blocks.title: Parkinson's-specific safety — read before starting
list: **Exercise during your 'on' time**, when your medication is working — usually 45 to 90 minutes after a dose. Exercising when you are 'off' is harder, less effective and more likely to end in a fall.

**Watch your blood pressure on standing.** Light-headedness on standing up is common in Parkinson's, and getting up quickly during exercise is exactly when it bites. Rise in stages, and tell me if it happens.
**Ballistic and power exercises need something to hold.** Fast movements plus impaired balance is the highest-risk combination on this page. Bench, wall or chair, always.
**If you freeze, do not fight it.** Use the strategies below rather than trying to push through — pushing through is how people fall forwards.
**Tell me if you have fallen.** Falls in Parkinson's are common, and the reasons are often treatable: medication timing, blood pressure, freezing, or the dose itself.

blocks.title: Why 'big, fast and difficult' is the prescription
blocks.lede: The principles below come from the neuroplasticity research that underpins PD Warrior and LSVT BIG. They explain why the exercises on this page look the way they do.

cards.title: Amplitude
body: Train movements that are deliberately too big. Your internal calibration is set too small, so 'too big' is what produces normal.

cards.title: Power and speed
body: Parkinson's slows the starting and the speed of movement more than it weakens muscle. Explosive, ballistic movement trains precisely the deficit.

cards.title: High effort
body: Comfortable exercise produces little. The trials that changed outcomes worked people hard — up to 80–85% of maximum heart rate.

cards.title: Frequency
body: Little and often, and permanently. The benefits fade within weeks of stopping, in every trial that has looked.

cards.title: Complexity
body: Add thinking, changes of direction, changes of rhythm. A complicated task engages far more of the brain than a repetitive one.

cards.title: Salience and enjoyment
body: The brain rewires around movements that matter to you. This is not sentimentality — it is why an exercise you enjoy outperforms one you endure, and why group classes work.

blocks.title: Part 1 — Think BIG
blocks.subtitle: Start every session here. Five minutes, and it sets the calibration for everything that follows.

blocks.title: Part 2 — Ballistic and power work
blocks.subtitle: The PD Warrior element: fast, explosive, deliberately effortful. Three days a week.

blocks.title: Part 3 — Aerobic exercise
blocks.subtitle: The part with the most interesting evidence of all. Four days a week.

blocks.title: Part 4 — Balance
blocks.subtitle: Because most of what causes harm in Parkinson's, causes it by way of a fall.

set.dose: Build to 15–30 seconds each leg, with hand support, daily

set.progression: Fingertips off the wall; then adding a big deliberate arm swing; then walking heel-to-toe to a beat you count out loud.

blocks.title: Part 5 — Complexity, freezing and real life
blocks.subtitle: The bridge between the exercises and the day.

blocks.title: A week that covers all of it
blocks.lede: This is more than most people start with. Build up to it over a couple of months — begin with Parts 1 and 2, three days a week.

blocks.title: Doing this with other people
blocks.lede: Home exercise works. Supervised and group exercise works better, and people keep doing it for longer.

items.title: PD Warrior
body: An Australian programme built around exactly the principles on this page, delivered by accredited physiotherapists and exercise physiologists, with classes across the country and an online option. Ask me for a referral, or look for an accredited provider in your area.

items.title: LSVT BIG (and LSVT LOUD)
body: An intensive amplitude-training protocol — four sessions a week for four weeks with a certified therapist, plus daily homework. If your movements have become noticeably small, this is the most concentrated way to reset them. LSVT LOUD does the same job for a quiet voice.

items.title: Group classes
body: Boxing-style classes, dance for Parkinson's, Tai Chi and hydrotherapy all have a following and a growing evidence base, and all deliver the two things a sheet cannot: supervision and company.

items.title: Parkinson's NSW and equivalents
body: State Parkinson's organisations run support groups, exercise classes and a nurse helpline, and can tell you what exists near you. Your GP can also arrange subsidised allied health sessions — see below.

a: Possibly — and this is the most interesting question in the field. High-intensity treadmill exercise at 80–85% of maximum heart rate, four days a week, was tested in the SPARX2 trial in early Parkinson's: it proved safe, and the motor scores of the high-intensity group did not worsen over six months, while the control group's did. That is a promising signal rather than proof, and the larger SPARX3 trial was designed to answer it properly.
What is beyond argument is that exercise improves how you function now, and that the benefit fades when you stop.

items.q: "Should I exercise before or after my tablets?"
a: After. Aim for the window when your medication is clearly working, typically 45 to 90 minutes after a dose. If you are consistently 'off' when you want to exercise, that is a reason to review the timing of your doses with me rather than to exercise 'off'.

items.q: "I get very light-headed when I stand up quickly."
a: Common in Parkinson's, and treatable. Rise in stages — sit on the edge, count to ten, stand holding something, count to ten again. Increase your salt and fluid intake unless you have been told not to, and tell me: some of the medications used for Parkinson's contribute, and there are treatments for the blood pressure drop itself.

items.q: "Is it safe to do fast, explosive movements at my age?"
a: With something solid to hold, and during 'on' time — yes, and it is one of the most useful things you can do. Power fades faster than strength with both age and Parkinson's, and it is power that gets you out of a chair and stops you falling. If your balance is significantly impaired, do the ballistic work seated: you keep most of the benefit and lose the risk.

items.q: "I freeze in doorways. Is that laziness or fear?"
a: Neither. It is a failure of the brain's internal 'go' signal, and it responds to external cues rather than to effort — counting out loud, a beat, a line to step over, a deliberately huge first step. Practise the strategies in Part 5 when you are *not* frozen, so they are automatic when you are. And tell me when it happens, because freezing that appears as a dose wears off is often treatable by adjusting the medication.

items.q: "My handwriting has shrunk and my voice has gone quiet. Is that the same problem?"
a: Yes — the same loss of amplitude, in the hand and in the voice. Both respond to the same 'go bigger' training. Practise big writing daily, and ask me about a speech pathology referral for the voice; LSVT LOUD is very effective for it.

items.q: "How long before I notice a difference?"
a: Most people notice something within four to six weeks, and the trials generally ran for eight to twelve weeks or longer. The honest catch is that the gains disappear if you stop, so the aim is a routine you can sustain for years, not a course you complete.

blocks.title: Tell me if
list: You have had a fall, or you are having near-falls or freezing episodes that are new or worsening.
You feel light-headed on standing, or you have blacked out.
Your symptoms fluctuate markedly through the day — this usually means the medication timing needs adjusting.
You are getting involuntary writhing or fidgety movements (dyskinesia), especially if they interfere with exercise.
Your voice is becoming quiet, or you are coughing or choking on food or drink.
Exercise consistently makes you feel unwell, breathless out of proportion, or brings on chest pain.
Your mood has dropped, or you have stopped doing things you used to enjoy — depression and apathy are part of Parkinson's, and both are treatable.
